competition.title: Orbit Wars
competition.metric: Ongoing Gaussian skill rating from ladder game outcomes; win margin does not affect rating updates

task_fingerprint.data: Variable-length planet, fleet and comet entities in 1v1 and four-player FFA episodes

summary: The leading Orbit Wars solution scaled pure self-play PPO to a 200M-parameter entity transformer and roughly 15B environment steps. Its strongest reusable lesson is systems-level co-design: structured target actions, one-pass multi-player modeling, a Rust vector environment verified against Kaggle replays, last-best checkpoint evaluation and distillation, distributed training, and deployment-aware quantization/fallback. The write-up also supplies unusually valuable negative evidence on gamma=1 stalling, matchup-distribution shift, action masks, three-bit quantization and missing league play.

validated_lessons.title: Scale model capacity only after simulator and PPO correctness are established
validated_lessons.mechanism: A high-throughput simulator and expressive transformer let additional model capacity and self-play steps absorb complex game dynamics that a small hand-engineered policy could not.
validated_lessons.implementation: Prototype with 1-5M parameter models, then scale to a 200M, 38-layer, 768-dimensional, 16-head transformer trained for about 15B self-play steps with distributed PPO.

effect.author_report: Performance improved markedly at each model-size increase; the final agent reached the top leaderboard position.
effect.training_cost: Approximately 2400 B200 GPU-hours for the final model.

transfer_conditions: Simulator throughput is high and parity-tested
Checkpoint evaluation is stable enough to detect progress
Compute and deployment compression budgets are available
failure_conditions: Low-budget settings cannot infer that the same scaling curve will hold
Scaling before validating the environment can amplify simulator or reward bugs
validated_lessons.minimal_next_test: Hold the simulator and training recipe fixed and compare a small geometric model-size ladder using a fixed opponent matrix.

validated_lessons.title: Keep observations low-level while factorizing an intractable action space
validated_lessons.mechanism: Selecting a semantic target entity removes difficult continuous geometric search while retaining entity-level state information and a continuous fleet-size decision.
validated_lessons.implementation: Replace raw launch-angle prediction with source-target attention over valid planets, then condition an eight-component truncated logistic mixture on the selected target to sample fleet size.

effect.author_report: The raw-angle policy remained far from competitive; the target-based action representation became the final approach.

transfer_conditions: Actions naturally decompose into candidate selection and magnitude
A deterministic converter can map the semantic target back to legal low-level controls
failure_conditions: A poor candidate generator can hide valid actions
Target abstraction may remove strategically important continuous degrees of freedom
validated_lessons.minimal_next_test: Compare raw controls and target-factorized actions under the same model size, environment steps and opponent set.

validated_lessons.title: Use a shared entity-token transformer for all players
validated_lessons.mechanism: Player, global, actor-plan, critic-value and scratch tokens share context with all entities, allowing symmetric multi-player decisions and values from one trunk execution.
validated_lessons.implementation: Project planets, fleets and comets to a shared hidden dimension; concatenate player/global/scratch/actor/critic tokens; run one transformer; decode each player's actor and winner probability.

effect.author_report: All players could be evaluated in one forward pass, saving roughly 2-4x compute relative to one observation per player.

transfer_conditions: Players share rules and observation schema
Entity order can be represented with masks rather than fixed slots
failure_conditions: Asymmetric roles may need explicit role tokens or separate adapters
Quadratic attention cost can dominate when entity counts become very large
validated_lessons.minimal_next_test: Compare one shared multi-player forward against per-player inference at equal parameters and measure throughput plus policy quality.

validated_lessons.title: Rewrite the simulator only with replay-level parity gates
validated_lessons.mechanism: A Rust vector environment increases rollout throughput, while reference-transition tests prevent silent divergence from Kaggle's Python game implementation.
validated_lessons.implementation: Run environments and observation writes in parallel with Rayon, reuse pinned Python buffers, and replay real Kaggle transitions through the Rust rules engine before comparing complete state and terminal results.

effect.author_report: The Python environment was too slow for RL; the Rust rewrite enabled large-scale parallel self-play.

transfer_conditions: Reference transitions or replays can be captured
The accelerated simulator exposes deterministic injection points for random events
failure_conditions: A fast simulator without parity coverage can optimize the wrong game
Sparse fixtures may miss rare rule branches
validated_lessons.minimal_next_test: Require parity on multiple player counts and every rare event before accepting a simulator optimization.

validated_lessons.title: Promote checkpoints by opponent wins and reuse last-best as a teacher
validated_lessons.mechanism: A moving last-best checkpoint supplies a concrete self-play progress gate and a stabilizing policy/value target without introducing external demonstrations.
validated_lessons.implementation: Evaluate current versus last-best in mixed 1v1 and 2v2 games; replace last-best above 70% win rate; add teacher action KL and winner-distribution cross-entropy terms to PPO.

effect.author_report: The terms were used to stabilize training.

transfer_conditions: Head-to-head or team evaluation is representative
The game is not strongly non-transitive over the selected opponent set
failure_conditions: One last-best opponent can miss strategic cycles
Four-player equilibria may require a league or historical opponent pool
validated_lessons.minimal_next_test: Compare last-best-only evaluation with an opponent matrix spanning several historical checkpoints.

validated_lessons.title: Co-design training, compression and runtime fallback
validated_lessons.mechanism: Submission quality is maximized by optimizing the complete constrained agent rather than the uncompressed training checkpoint in isolation.
validated_lessons.implementation: Use groupwise four-bit NormalFloat checkpoint compression, dynamic int8 CPU linear layers, bounded visible fleets and an overage-triggered 5M fallback model.

effect.slow_game_fraction: About 8% of four-player games required fallback on particularly slow CPUs.
effect.fallback_conversion: The author reported the 5M fallback converted 100% of positions the critic considered winning.
effect.quantized_head_to_head: The four-bit model won about 40% against the unquantized model; three-bit quality loss outweighed the benefit of a larger model.

transfer_conditions: The platform has strict package and per-action latency constraints
A smaller fallback policy can be packaged and initialized safely
failure_conditions: Aggressive entity pruning can remove decisive state
A critic-based fallback assumption can fail on poorly calibrated values
Lower-bit compression can lose more policy quality than extra parameters recover
validated_lessons.minimal_next_test: Benchmark full agents under the real CPU, package and timeout limits using replay-level action agreement and head-to-head games.

validated_lessons.title: Use coding agents as an implementation multiplier, not a research oracle
validated_lessons.mechanism: Agentic coding sharply reduces implementation latency in a greenfield, low-stakes competition, but architecture, experiments and branch selection still require human research judgment.
validated_lessons.implementation: Write explicit specifications and generated documentation, isolate risky branches, and discard failed codebases instead of endlessly layering experiments into one mutable tree.

effect.author_report: Preliminary experiments were running within a couple of weeks, but agent suggestions and creativity were not substitutes for thinking.
effect.discussion_report: Another participant reported that continually extending one agentic codebase eventually became unmanageable.

transfer_conditions: Cheap failure and strong automated tests
failure_conditions: Production systems with users, compatibility constraints or expensive mistakes
No branch isolation, review gates or deletion policy
validated_lessons.minimal_next_test: Compare isolated worktree branches against one cumulative branch on defect rate, experiment turnaround and rollback cost.

negative_lessons.title: Undiscounted returns encouraged stalling
negative_lessons.mechanism: With gamma=1, a winning policy had no incentive to finish early, so already-decided episodes consumed training compute.
negative_lessons.implementation: The 200M config uses gamma=1.0 to keep the multiplayer winner-probability critic well-defined.
failure_conditions: Long terminal horizons with sparse outcome rewards
negative_lessons.minimal_next_test: Test early truncation or surrender rules while verifying that policy ranking remains aligned with true wins.

negative_lessons.title: Short-term ladder composition was mistaken for the final opponent distribution
negative_lessons.mechanism: Raising the two-player training mixture to 90% and omitting league play overfit the observed pre-deadline matchmaking distribution; the top ladder later became four-player-heavy.
negative_lessons.implementation: Keep player-mode mixtures robust and evaluate against historical checkpoints or a league rather than one current opponent.
failure_conditions: Online matchmaking and final evaluation distributions can differ
Multiplayer self-play can cycle strategically
negative_lessons.minimal_next_test: Report a 2p/4p by opponent-checkpoint evaluation matrix before changing the training mixture.

negative_lessons.title: A hard mask for obviously bad launches reduced learned policy quality
negative_lessons.mechanism: Removing bad actions may also remove pressure to learn the underlying physics representation.
negative_lessons.implementation: Treat action masks as an ablation variable; the author later restored a mask for fine-tuning and inference rather than assuming one setting was universally best.
failure_conditions: The observation is not independently quantified and may be confounded by training stage or hyperparameters
negative_lessons.minimal_next_test: Run mask-on, mask-off and late-mask schedules with equal seeds and environment steps.

negative_lessons.title: Three-bit compression did not justify a larger model
negative_lessons.mechanism: Additional model capacity was outweighed by larger policy distortion from lower-bit quantization.
negative_lessons.implementation: Stop at four-bit NormalFloat after comparing the compressed policy head-to-head, not only by payload size.
failure_conditions: The exact crossover depends on architecture, codebook, group size and inference kernel
negative_lessons.minimal_next_test: Measure action agreement, value error, head-to-head win rate, size and latency for each bit-width.

negative_lessons.title: The current repository snapshot is not an immutable copy of the exact winning submission
negative_lessons.mechanism: The public repository continued evolving after the competition solution, so later LoRA, reward and quantization features cannot automatically be credited to the submitted agent.
negative_lessons.implementation: Use docs/write-up.md for solution claims, pin commit a60ec580 for reproducibility, and require a tagged submission artifact before attributing later features to the winning run.
failure_conditions: Attribution is unsafe when code history, checkpoint and packaged submission are not tied together
negative_lessons.minimal_next_test: Compare a released submission archive or tag against the pinned repository tree.

best_solution_lineage.change: Small 1-5M models, target-based actions, Rust simulator parity and PPO smoke tests
Increase transformer capacity and distributed self-play throughput
Last-best checkpoint gate plus teacher policy/value losses
NF4 checkpoint, CPU int8, entity filtering and 5M overage fallback

def _quantize_normalfloat_g128_lsq(
    tensor: torch.Tensor,
    bits: int,
) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
    _validate_normalfloat_bits(bits, "normalfloat", None)
    tensor = tensor.to(torch.float32)
    if tensor.ndim != 2:
        raise ValueError("normal-float groupwise quantization requires 2D tensors")
    if not torch.isfinite(tensor).all().item():
        raise ValueError("normal-float groupwise quantization requires finite tensors")

    rows, cols = tensor.shape
    group_count = (cols + _NORMALFLOAT_GROUP_SIZE - 1) // _NORMALFLOAT_GROUP_SIZE
    padded_cols = group_count * _NORMALFLOAT_GROUP_SIZE
    padded = torch.zeros((rows, padded_cols), dtype=torch.float32, device=tensor.device)
    padded[:, :cols] = tensor
    groups = padded.reshape(rows * group_count, _NORMALFLOAT_GROUP_SIZE)
    valid = torch.zeros((rows, padded_cols), dtype=torch.bool, device=tensor.device)
    valid[:, :cols] = True
    valid_groups = valid.reshape(rows * group_count, _NORMALFLOAT_GROUP_SIZE)

    valid_abs_groups = torch.where(valid_groups, groups.abs(), torch.zeros_like(groups))
    max_abs = valid_abs_groups.amax(dim=1, keepdim=True)
    scale = max_abs
    values = _normalfloat_values_for_bits(bits).to(device=tensor.device)
    thresholds = _normalfloat_thresholds_for_bits(bits).to(device=tensor.device)
    for _ in range(2):
        safe_scale = torch.where(scale == 0, torch.ones_like(scale), scale)
        codes = torch.bucketize(groups / safe_scale, thresholds).to(torch.long)
        quantized = values[codes]
        valid_quantized = torch.where(
            valid_groups,
            quantized,
            torch.zeros_like(quantized),
        )
        valid_group_values = torch.where(valid_groups, groups, torch.zeros_like(groups))
        denominator = (valid_quantized * valid_quantized).sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)
        raw_improved = (valid_group_values * valid_quantized).sum(
            dim=1, keepdim=True
        ) / denominator
